hook.support: You did the work. Now show it off. A great showcase is short, clear and real. Your slides help. Your voice tells the story.
hook.core: You’ve done the work. Now it’s time to show it off, to your class, your family, or people from your community. A great showcase isn’t a wall of words on a screen. It’s you telling the story of what you did and what you learnt, with pictures doing the heavy lifting.
hook.extend: A showcase is where your project goes public. It’s a short talk that shows what you set out to do, what you found and what you learnt. Done well, it’s the part of the project people remember. Research on slides shows how to make it work.

why.support: Showing your work is a job skill. People remember a good talk.
why.core: Presenting your work is something you’ll do in job interviews, at TAFE and at work. A clear, well-built presentation gets your effort noticed.
why.extend: Every workplace and course values people who can present their work clearly. That means honest credit for sources, and visuals that help rather than distract.

articles.title: Build a showcase people remember

body.support:
Your showcase is a short talk about your project. Aim for **3 to 5 minutes**.

**Put it in order.**
1. **Hook.** Start with a photo, a question or a surprising fact.
2. **My question.** What did you want to find out or make?
3. **What I did.** Show the steps. Photos help.
4. **What I found.** The most interesting thing.
5. **What I learnt.** About the topic, and about yourself. What would you do next time?
.
**Make simple slides.**
- One idea per slide.
- Big pictures. Only a few words.
- Don’t read your slides out. You do the talking.
.
**Credit everything.** Say where facts came from. Credit photos you didn’t take. Using someone else’s work as your own is **plagiarism**. Add a **credits slide** at the end.

**Use your body and voice.** Look up. Slow down. Pause before important bits.
body.core:
Your showcase is a short, **informative** presentation about your project, about **3 to 5 minutes**, with slides, a video, photos or objects to support it.

**Sequence it.** A clear order keeps your audience with you.
1. **Hook:** a photo, a question or a surprising fact.
2. **My question:** what you set out to find out or make, and why.
3. **What I did:** the main steps, shown with photos or video.
4. **What I found:** your most interesting findings or results.
5. **What I learnt:** about the topic and about yourself. What went well? What would you change? What’s next?
.
**Make slides that help.** Your slides support you; they don’t replace you.
- One idea per slide.
- Big pictures, a few key words, large text.
- Never read full sentences off the screen.
.
**Credit every source.** **Plagiarism** is using someone else’s words, ideas, photos, music or video as if they were yours. To avoid it:
- put your research into your own words, and say where it came from: “According to the Your Career website…”.
- use your own photos, or images you’re allowed to use, and credit them.
- finish with a **credits slide** listing every source.
.
**Deliver it.** Use what you learnt in Body Talk: steady stance, eye contact around the room, gestures, pace and pauses. Practise twice with your slides.

**Take questions.** Thank the person, answer briefly, and it’s fine to say “I didn’t find that out, but I could.”
body.extend:
Your showcase is a short **informative** presentation, around **3 to 5 minutes**, that shares your project and your learning, supported by a **digital, multimodal or visual** platform: slides, video, photos, a poster or physical objects.

**Sequence for engagement.**
1. **Hook:** an image, question or striking fact that earns attention.
2. **Focus:** your question or goal, and why it mattered to you.
3. **Process:** what you did, shown rather than told.
4. **Findings:** the most significant or surprising results.
5. **Reflection and review:** what you learnt about the topic and about yourself, what worked, what you’d change, and what comes next.
.
**Design support that complements speech.** Research on multimedia learning suggests that audiences learn less when slides duplicate your words exactly, because reading and listening compete for attention. Short key words, images and simple charts work better. One idea per slide; large, readable text.

**Acknowledge sources.** **Plagiarism** is presenting others’ words, ideas or media as your own. Avoid it by paraphrasing and attributing (“The Victorian Skills Gateway lists…”), using your own or properly licensed images, and closing with a **credits slide** that lists every source.

**Deliver deliberately.** Apply the delivery tools from Body Talk: stance, distributed eye contact, purposeful gesture, controlled pace and pauses. Rehearse with the slides at least twice.

**Handle questions.** Listen fully, answer concisely, and be honest about the limits of what you found.

caseStudies.title: Read the slide or listen to me?

body.support:
Scientists have tested how people learn from slides and talking.

In one study from 2013, people watched a short lesson. Some saw **every word** on screen while it was read out. Others saw **only a few key words**.

The people who saw **every word** learned **less**. It’s hard to read and listen at the same time.

The people with a **few key words** did better.

Here’s the twist. Many people said they **liked** the full text more. But it didn’t help them learn.
body.core:
Scientists who study learning have tested what happens when slides show the same words someone is saying out loud.

An earlier line of research, led by psychologist Richard Mayer, found that people often learn **less** when on-screen text repeats the narration word for word. Reading and listening at the same time compete for your attention.

In **2013**, researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) took it further. People watched a short narrated lesson. Some saw the **full text** of the narration on screen. Others saw a **shortened version**: just the key words.

The full-text group learned **less**. A short, slightly different version on screen worked better.

And here’s the twist: many people **preferred** the full text, even though it didn’t help them learn.

For your showcase, the lesson is clear. Put a few key words and strong pictures on your slides, and do the talking yourself.
body.extend:
Researchers have tested many times what happens when on-screen text repeats what a speaker says. Work led by psychologist Richard Mayer found that people often learn **less** when the same words are on screen and spoken. This is called the **redundancy effect**. Reading and listening to the same words compete for your attention.

In **2013**, a team at UCLA (Yue, Bjork and Bjork) looked closer. People watched a short narrated lesson. Some saw the **full text** of the narration on screen. Others saw a **shortened** version with only key words. The full text hurt learning. A small difference between screen and speech actually helped.

Here’s the twist. Many people **preferred** the full text and believed it helped them, even though it didn’t. What feels easier isn’t always what works.

For presenters, the lesson is practical. Slides should support your speech, not copy it. Key words, images and clear visuals help an audience. Paragraphs read aloud get in the way.

source.name: Yue, Bjork & Bjork (2013), study of on-screen text and narration, Journal of Educational Psychology (PDF, UCLA Bjork Learning and Forgetting Lab)

model.text:
**Opening (slide: a photo of a muddy BMX track)**

“Forty minutes. That’s how far I ride to the nearest pump track. My project asked one question: what would it take to build one here?”

**Closing (slide: “What I learnt” and three key words)**

“I learnt that a track costs more than I thought, but there might be grants that could help. I also learnt I can pick up the phone and talk to someone important. I was nervous calling the youth officer, and she was great.

Next, I’m taking my plan to the youth council.

The photos are mine. The cost figures are from the council website. They’re on my credits slide. Thanks for listening. Any questions?”
why: The opening hooks with a real number and states the question straight away.
The closing reflects on the topic **and** on the student’s own growth, then says what’s next.
It credits sources out loud and invites questions.

teacher.overview: The culminating VPC Literacy presentation (Unit 4 Module 1). Students sequence an informative 3–5 minute presentation (hook, question, what I did, what I found, what I learnt), design slides or visuals that complement speech, acknowledge every source with a credits slide, deliver with deliberate body language and voice, take questions, and reflect on their learning. The case study is research on slide design: identical on-screen text reduced learning compared with a few key words (Yue, Bjork & Bjork, 2013, building on Mayer’s redundancy research).
prep: Book the showcase: a class session, a lunchtime event, or an evening with families or community partners. A real audience matters.
Check presentation tech (projector, clicker, audio) in the room beforehand.
Students should have their project from Pitch Your Project, or another substantial piece of work from VPC (a reel, zine or campaign).

**Check & sign-off:** quick check, reflection page, sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Sort:** paragraph read aloud — needs work; big photo + four words — good; uncredited web photo — needs work; credits slide — good; ten tiny bullet points — needs work; simple labelled chart — good.

**Annotation:** 1 hook (picture + question); 2 focus question and why; 3 process shown with photos and video; 4 findings as one clear visual; 5 reflection and next step; 6 credits for every source.

**Case study:** the full-text group learned less than the key-words group; many people preferred full text even though it didn’t help; use key words and images, and do the talking.

realityCheck: **A real audience changes everything.** Even inviting one other class or a few parents raises the effort level. Book it early and tell students who’s coming.

**Some students will be very anxious.** Offer a smaller audience, presenting with a partner, or a recorded presentation (the solo option). The learning is in the planning and reflection as much as the delivery.
**Tech fails.** Have every presentation saved in one place, and a plan B (print the key photos).
**Students over-fill slides.** The hook demonstration (the wordy slide read aloud) usually fixes it faster than any rule.
**Works in a real class:** yes, and it’s often the highlight of the year. Celebrate it.

levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 9 reading: multimodal design, the redundancy effect and its limits, attribution, and explaining technical vocabulary.
